title: Warning: Most Teachers Make This Classroom Management Mistake; Do You?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a common mistake he sees teachers make when responding to misbehavior: asking students to explain why they misbehaved. Through an extended dialogue example, he shows how demanding an explanation from a student standing on a chair produces frustration for the teacher and resentment in the student, without actually addressing the misbehavior. He argues the question is counterproductive for several reasons: the teacher already knows the real answer (the student wanted to), students rarely answer honestly, the confrontation substitutes for an actual consequence, it breeds resentment, it wastes classroom time, and it's needlessly stressful. His recommended alternative is brief and consequence-based: state the rule violation and the consequence in just a few words, then move on without further discussion. He notes one exception—when a student's behavior might involve bullying or retaliation, asking why can be appropriate to rule out a deeper issue.
points: Asking students why they misbehaved is a common but counterproductive habit that breeds resentment without improving behavior.
Teachers already know the real answer to 'why'—because at the time, the student wanted to—so the question is largely rhetorical and unproductive.
Demanding an explanation substitutes for an actual consequence and wastes valuable classroom time and momentum.
The better approach: state the broken rule and the resulting consequence in just a few words, then move on immediately.
One exception exists: asking why can be appropriate when ruling out bullying or retaliation as an underlying cause of misbehavior.
quotes: The mistake most teachers make is asking students why they misbehaved.
Jeffrey hems and haws and, like anyone caught behaving poorly, is not sure how to answer.
The reason Jeffery made the decision to stand on his chair is the same reason any of us behaves poorly: because, at the time, he wanted to.
Forcing an explanation from students causes resentment. To them it feels like humiliation. Yes, you have a right to handle misbehavior this way. But you’ll pay a price for it.
A better way to handle misbehavior is to hold students accountable with a consequence.
Four words, three seconds, one consequence and Mr. Shoemaker was done with the interaction.
If you notice a student lashing out against others, you may have to ask why in order to rule out retaliation against bullying—which can never be taken lightly.
